aboutDescription: O Tempora is an interactive timeline of world history — People, Conflicts, and Milestones, spanning ~800 BCE to the present.
aboutCodeBody: This site's source code is open source, licensed under the MIT License.
aboutDataPeopleBody: People data is drawn from Pantheon 2.0 by Datawheel, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Descriptions are additionally sourced from Wikidata (CC0).
aboutDataEventsBody: Conflicts and Milestones data is drawn from Wikidata, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
helpTravelBody: Drag sideways, or swipe on a phone, to move through time. Hold Shift and scroll to pan too. Zoom with the + and − buttons, Ctrl or ⌘ and scroll, or by pinching.
helpMarksBody: A line is a life or a stretch of time; a dot is a single moment. People sit above the year ruler, conflicts and milestones below it.
helpColorsBody: A person's color shows their field, as listed under Occupation in the filters. Conflicts are red; milestones are green or gold.
helpDetailLevelBody: Sets how much is shown. Legendary shows only the best known; Deep Cut adds the long tail.
helpDetailsBody: Select a name or a dot to read about it and open its Wikipedia page.
helpKeysBody: ← and → pan (add Shift to go further). + and − zoom. Press ? to open this help and Esc to close it.
detailLevelDescription.legendary: Only top-tier, world-altering figures, major conflicts, and pivotal milestones.
detailLevelDescription.mainstream: Essential historical figures, key conflicts, and primary milestones.
detailLevelDescription.specialized: Includes notable figures, secondary conflicts, and regional milestones.
detailLevelDescription.deep-cut: Displays high-density details, including niche figures, minor conflicts, and obscure milestones.
landingPitch: People, conflicts and milestones from about 800 BCE to today, side by side on one axis.
landingCase.shelley-summer.lede: Mary Shelley began Frankenstein in the year without a summer.
landingCase.shelley-summer.caption: Rain kept the guests indoors by Lake Geneva in 1816. Lord Byron challenged each of them to write a ghost story.
landingCase.vermeer-leeuwenhoek.lede: The man who studied life in a drop of water also settled the debts of Vermeer’s household.
landingCase.vermeer-leeuwenhoek.caption: In 1676, Delft’s magistrates appointed the microscope maker Antonie van Leeuwenhoek to administer the estate of Vermeer’s widow.
landingCase.einstein-szilard.lede: Einstein and Szilárd patented a refrigerator that ran on heat.
landingCase.einstein-szilard.caption: The first household refrigerator dates to 1913. The two physicists received their US patent in 1930 for a design with no moving parts.
landingCase.october-calendar.lede: By the Gregorian calendar, the October Revolution began in November.
landingCase.october-calendar.caption: Russia still used the Julian calendar in 1917. October 25 in Petrograd was November 7 on the Gregorian calendar.
landingCase.tolstoy-gandhi.lede: Gandhi wrote to Tolstoy about a South African farm that bore the writer’s name.
landingCase.tolstoy-gandhi.caption: Their correspondence began in 1909. The following year Gandhi sent news of Tolstoy Farm, a home for families taking part in his campaign.
landingCase.charlemagne-elephant.lede: Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne an elephant named Abul-Abbas.
landingCase.charlemagne-elephant.caption: In July 802, the envoy Isaac reached Aachen with the caliph’s gift. The Frankish annals recorded the elephant’s name.
landingCase.curie-x-rays.lede: Marie Curie brought X-rays to wartime hospitals in a car that powered its own equipment.
landingCase.curie-x-rays.caption: X-rays were discovered in 1895. During World War I, a dynamo driven by the car’s engine powered the machine that helped doctors locate shrapnel.
landingFooterData: Data from Pantheon 2.0, Wikidata and Wikipedia.
